title: A forest student
hookLine: Ajahn Chah, Ajahn Mun's student in spirit, whose forest monastery welcomed Western monks

lines: LET IN AND HANDED A BROOM.
cards: A young man from the West stands at the gate of a forest monastery in Thailand, newly ordained or hoping to be. He doesn't speak the language. He doesn't know the chants.
He isn't sure how to wrap a robe or where to leave his sandals. The teacher could easily tell him to come back when he knows more.
Instead, as the story is told, he's let in and put to work: sweeping leaves off the paths, hauling water, walking for alms with everyone else. The teacher was Ajahn Chah.

teach.b: First, a student in spirit. Tradition says Ajahn Chah spent only a short time with Ajahn Mun, yet that meeting stayed with him.

Afterward he wandered and practiced in the forests the way Mun had, and in time settled in a forest near his home village, where a monastery grew up around him. Not long years at Mun's side, but the same forest way.
Accounts describe him speaking in plain village language, with jokes and everyday pictures: a glass of muddy water settling, a leaf stirred by the wind.
When students complained about the heat, the food or each other, he'd turn the complaint around. The trouble, he suggested, wasn't the heat. It was the wanting it to be different.
Western monks came, and he didn't build them an easier track.

teach.h: AN OPEN GATE, THE SAME PATH.
teach.b: They ate the same food, kept the same hours, swept the same paths and sat through the same restless nights.
In time a monastery was set up near his own, Wat Pah Nanachat, where newcomers from abroad could train with teaching in English. Fourth, what welcome means here.
Not lowering the bar, but opening the gate and walking beside the newcomer through the same hard days. The forest welcomed them, and it didn't change for them.
Monasteries started later by his Western students carry the same pattern into other countries.

how: Monasteries in Ajahn Chah's lineage, in Thailand and in other countries, follow the forest routine of alms round, work and meditation, and welcome lay visitors and guests who wish to stay and practice.

games.why: as the story is told, newcomers were let in and given the same forest life as everyone else, with no easier track.

practice: Bring back a time you were the newcomer, at a job, a school, a family dinner where you knew nobody, and remember what helped: someone who showed you where things were, someone who didn't make you feel slow.
Breathe with that memory for a moment. Then hold in mind someone who's new in your life right now, for a few easy breaths.

wordCard.voice: Acariya. The Pali word for teacher, the root of the Thai title ajahn, given to teachers like Ajahn Chah who welcomed students from abroad. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali acariya: teacher. the Thai title ajahn is usually traced to it.

carryVoice: Your line: the forest welcomed them. An open gate, and the same path for all. Back tomorrow, same hill.
